title:
We’ll give him a ragging worse than they gave Clive Kempthorpe.
 
 Young shouts of moneyed voices in Clive Kempthorpe’s rooms. Palefaces: they hold their ribs with laughter, one clasping another. O, I shall expire! Break the news to her gently, Aubrey! I shall die! With slit ribbons of his shirt whipping the air he hops and hobbles round the table, with trousers down at heels, chased by Ades of Magdalen with the tailor’s shears. A scared calf’s face gilded with marmalade. I don’t want to be debagged! Don’t you play the giddy ox with me!
html_source:
Stephen has complained to Mulligan about their visitor, Haines, and Mulligan has threatened some violence against him if he acts up again. This has led Stephen to a sequence of thoughts about Mulligan’s real or imagined hazing of someone named Clive Kempthorpe, involving at least the threat of castration with shears: “debagged”.

While some might not think it means that, you might be appalled when you study the text further:

With slit ribbons of his shirt whipping the air, he hops and hobbles round the table, with trousers down at heels, chased by Ades of Magdalen with the tailor’s shears. A scared calf’s face gilded with marmalade.

In this descriptive scene of terror, Buck talks about shredding Haines' shirt with shears and dropping his pants to his ankles as he chases after him with the shears; his face being covered with sweat because he is fearful of his life.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: “Debagged” = having your trousers removed by force.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I think the hazing being described here is by English boys in a prep school against Clive Kempthorpe. The mention of “moneyed” voices and pale faces would suggest that. Also the “giddy ox” along side the term debugging would suggest threat of castration.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Not a prep school: Magdalen is an Oxford College

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I might also mention the very similar debagging scene at the beginning of Evelyn Waugh’s ‘Decline & Fall’ and add that Oxbridge Colleges have quadrangles. When Joyce refers to Mathew Arnold he may be thinking of Arnold’s poem ‘The Scholar Gypsy’ about an Oxford student who deserts his studies to follow the gypsies.
